help.intro: Possessive articles say whose something is — mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr — and they behave exactly like ein: they take the ein-endings, decided by the noun that follows, not by the owner. So mein Vater (masculine), mein Kind (neuter), meine Mutter (feminine), meine Eltern (plural); and in the accusative the masculine adds -en: Ich sehe meinen Vater. The owner only decides which word you start from: sein for his (and for its with a der/das-word), ihr for her (and for their), Ihr with a capital for your (formal). Choose the owner, then add the ending for the noun — two separate decisions, in that order.
help.tips[0].title: Pick the owner
help.tips[0].text: ich → mein · du → dein · er/es → sein · sie (she) → ihr · wir → unser · ihr (you all) → euer · sie (they) → ihr · Sie → Ihr.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: That's Tom. His car is new.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: That's Anna. Her car is old.
help.tips[0].check.q: Ben und ich lernen Deutsch. ____ Lehrer heißt Herr Wolf. (Our teacher …)
help.tips[0].check.why: The owners are wir (Ben and I), and wir → unser. euer belongs to ihr (you all).
help.tips[0].visual.columns[0].label: owner word
help.tips[1].title: Then add the ein-ending for the noun
help.tips[1].text: Nominative: no ending for masculine and neuter (mein Vater, mein Kind); -e for feminine and plural (meine Mutter, meine Kinder). Accusative: masculine adds -en (meinen Vater), the rest as in the nominative.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: My sister is called Mia. I see my sister. (feminine: same both times)
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: My brother is here. I see my brother. (masculine: -en as object)
help.tips[1].check.q: Ich suche ____ Schlüssel. (der Schlüssel, my key)
help.tips[1].check.why: Schlüssel is masculine and the object of suchen, so it takes -en, exactly like einen.
help.tips[1].visual.caption: The ending comes from the noun, exactly as with ein.
help.tips[2].text: sein looks like 'sie' but means his; ihr means her (and their). Decide by the owner's gender, never by the noun's: Anna und ihr Bruder; Tom und seine Schwester.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: Anna and her dog. Tom and his dog.
help.tips[2].trap: 'sein' ≠ 'sie'. English speakers map sein → she; it is the opposite: sein = his.
help.tips[2].check.q: Herr Becker ruft ____ Tochter an. (his daughter)
help.tips[2].check.why: The owner is a man, so his = sein; Tochter is feminine, so it gets -e: seine Tochter.
help.tips[2].visual.caption: The owner decides sein or ihr; the noun decides the ending.
help.tips[3].title: euer loses an e
help.tips[3].text: With an ending, euer drops its second e: eure Mutter, euren Vater, eure Kinder. unser keeps everything: unsere Mutter.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: Where is your (pl.) teacher? Is that your house?
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: We're visiting your father and your children.
help.tips[3].check.why: Schuhe is plural, so the possessive takes -e, and euer drops its second e: eure.
help.remember[0]: Owner first, noun second: 'sein/ihr' comes from the owner, the ending comes from the noun.
help.remember[1]: A possessive is an ein-word — whatever ein does, mein does too.
help.context.en: This is my family. My father works in Bonn, my mother is a doctor. My sister has a dog – her dog is called Bello. My brother has a cat; his cat is black. And our house? It's small, but we love our house.
help.mistakes[0].why: The owner is female, so her = ihr; sein is his.
help.mistakes[1].why: Masculine object takes -en, exactly like einen.
help.mistakes[2].why: Neuter takes no ending in the nominative and accusative.
help.hook: Say whose things are whose — mein, dein, sein, ihr — and get the ending right by looking at the noun, not the owner.
categories[1].label: dein (your, Nom.)
